current_text.html: The time having come for the making of a public profession, and those who have been approved by the Session having taken their places in the presence of the congregation, the minister may state that: Of the number of those who were baptized in infancy as members of the Church of God by birthright, and as heirs of the covenant promises, the Session has examined and approved (call them by name), who come now to assume for themselves the full privileges and responsibilities of their inheritance in the household of faith. If there be present any candidates for Baptism, the minister may state that: As applicants for admission into the Church of God by Baptism, which is a sign and seal of our engrafting into Christ, and of our engagement to be the Lord's, the Session has examined and approved (call them by name), who are cordially welcomed into the fellowship of the household of faith. The minister may then address those making a profession in the following terms: (All of) you being here present to make a public profession of faith, are to assent to the following declarations and promises, by which you enter into a solemn covenant with God and His Church. 1. Do you acknowledge yourselves to be sinners in the sight of God, justly deserving His displeasure, and without hope save in His sovereign mercy? 2. Do you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ as the Son of God, and Savior of sinners, and do you receive and rest upon Him alone for salvation as He is offered in the Gospel? 3. Do you now resolve and promise, in humble reliance upon the grace of the Holy Spirit, that you will endeavor to live as becomes the followers of Christ? 4. Do you promise to support the Church in its worship and work to the best of your ability? 5. Do you submit yourselves to the government and discipline of the Church, and promise to study its purity and peace? The minister may now briefly admonish those making a profession of faith as to the importance of the solemn obligations they have assumed; then baptism may be administered, if there be present any candidates for the ordinance, and the whole concluded with prayer.

relationships.title: Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. The decision did not annul the completed ordination/installation, but required future elections and installations to comply with the Constitution.

metadata.synopsis: The SJC sustained an appeal by seven members of a 38-member mission church who were convicted by their temporary Session of opposing the organizing minister's expected election as pastor. Reversing the Presbytery's affirmance and the guilty verdicts underlying indefinite suspensions, the SJC held the indictments fatally lacked BCO 32-5 specificity; Presbytery used the wrong standard of review; the Session had no authority to control pastoral selection; and no Fifth or Ninth Commandment offense was proved. Challenges to witness-judges, venue, and refusal to refer were rejected.

metadata.synopsis: Members challenged a voting restriction imposed at a congregational meeting. The SJC dismissed the complaint as judicially out of order because BCO 43-1 permits complaints against acts or decisions of church courts, and a congregation is not such a court. It identified other possible routes through a report to Presbytery or review of church records. The adopted decision did not decide whether the voting restriction was constitutionally valid.

metadata.synopsis: A church member appealed Presbytery’s affirmance of his conviction and excommunication for failing to heed Session admonition and membership vows, including prolonged absence from that church. The SJC affirmed and denied the appeal, holding that all four specifications—lack of reasonable indulgence, haste, prejudice, and injustice—were nonspecific and unsupported. It emphasized his admissions that the charges were true, the adequate timeline, and the bar on considering evidence not offered at trial. A dissent disputed his PCA membership, standing, and the Session’s jurisdiction.

metadata.synopsis: At issue was whether North Texas Presbytery wrongly denied a complaint challenging Fort Worth Presbyterian Church’s “Special Case Felons” integration policy as contrary to Scripture. The SJC denied the complaint, holding that the complainant did not show the Session violated Scripture or the Constitution and that BCO 39-3.3 required deference absent clear error, leaving the lower-court actions in effect. The decision, adopted 20-1, expressly did not endorse the Respondents’ Preliminary Principles arguments; a concurrence disclaimed approval of the policy, and one member dissented.

metadata.synopsis: A member removed from the rolls under BCO 38-4 challenged Presbytery's ruling that she lacked standing to complain because she was no longer a member. The SJC sustained the complaint: standing under BCO 43-1 cannot be defeated by the very removal challenged. Removal under BCO 38-4 is pastoral discipline, a disciplinary case, not a merely administrative act. The SJC remanded to Presbytery to consider the complaint and take the action it should have taken—remand to the Session. The merits of the removal were not decided.

metadata.synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 matter, the SJC held that a presbytery erred in upholding a session's erasure of a member who pled not guilty to failing to submit and pursued divorce. The session wrongly equated declining divorce counsel with refusing submission, failed to assess membership duties in another branch, failed to notify her of erasure, and proceeded without process after dropping charges. The SJC sustained the challenge, directed the session to note the notice failure and remove her under BCO 38-3(a), but ordered no express reversal.

relationships.title: Memorial of Central Carolina v. Louisiana

metadata.synopsis: In a BCO 40-5 memorial, Central Carolina Presbytery alleged that Louisiana Presbytery had exonerated TE J. Steven Wilkins despite his published views on election, the church, perseverance, assurance, and baptism allegedly contradicting the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the memorial’s gravity and found Presbytery failed to show due diligence, ordering a recorded examination, formal responses, and report. Presbytery later met the procedural directives, but the SJC relied on Case 2007-8’s substantive finding, cited Presbytery under BCO 40-5, and appointed a prosecutor for Case 2007-14.

topics: peace and purity of the church
metadata.synopsis: Members challenged Presbytery’s denial of their complaint against a Session instruction not to circulate an open letter repeating allegations against their pastor. The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the instruction in force. It held that liberty of conscience does not eliminate members’ obligation to obey lawful church injunctions. Here the members had sought the Session’s advice, Presbytery had found no strong presumption of chargeable offenses, and renewed circulation would disturb the church’s peace; under those circumstances, the Session acted within its authority.

metadata.synopsis: Black challenged Presbytery’s handling of his complaint and its ruling that a licentiate’s non-24-hour creation-day view was not an exception to the Westminster Standards. The SJC denied remand because Presbytery had effectively adjudicated the complaint; the separate objection to proceeding without Black was not first filed below and was administratively out of order. It upheld Presbytery’s ruling that not every non-Calendar-Day view constitutes an exception. Because the record did not identify the licentiate’s precise view, the decision did not determine its acceptability or whether it could be taught.

metadata.synopsis: A church member appealed convictions and excommunication arising from vulgar statements to two patients, challenging the lack of pretrial reconciliation, recusals, the prosecutor’s participation in deliberations, and Presbytery procedure. The SJC left guilt intact and denied a new trial, though it held that a prosecutor may not deliberate as a judge. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. It remanded only to impose indefinite suspension from the Sacraments and conditions pending satisfactory evidence of repentance.

metadata.synopsis: A member challenged Presbytery’s affirmance of his excommunication, contending that SJC Case 97-9 had reversed his four guilty verdicts and precluded increased censure. The SJC did not sustain either issue. Case 97-9 had reversed only the original censure, leaving guilt intact. Because the offender bore the burden of showing repentance, and Session’s contrary factual determination received great deference absent clear error, the later excommunication remained in effect.
